title: Arrays
goal: Arrays declare, traverse, search, sort aur 2D arrays handle karna.
objectives: Declare, initialise and traverse one- and two-dimensional arrays
Explain the difference between an array's length field and a String's length()
Search and sort an array with a loop and with java.util.Arrays
definition: An array is a fixed-size container of values of one type, stored contiguously and accessed by a zero-based index. Its length is fixed at creation. A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, so its rows may have different lengths (a jagged array).
explain: Arrays give you numbered slots. int[] marks = new int[5] creates five ints initialised to 0; the valid indexes are 0 to 4. Asking for marks[5] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because the last valid index is always length - 1.

Traversal is a loop from 0 to length - 1, or a for-each loop when you only need the values. For-each cannot change the array elements' positions or know the index, so a classic for is still needed for search positions.

A 2D array is an array whose elements are arrays. int[][] grid = new int[3][4] gives three rows of four columns, but int[][] jagged = new int[3][] lets each row have its own length. java.util.Arrays supplies sort, toString, equals, copyOf and binarySearch, which are safer than hand-rolled versions.
hinglish: Array numbered slots ka dabba hai. int[] marks = new int[5] paanch ints banata hai, sab 0 se shuru. Valid index 0 se 4 tak — marks[5] maangoge to ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aayega, kyunki last index length - 1 hota hai.
2D array asal me array of arrays hai, isliye har row ki length alag ho sakti hai (jagged). java.util.Arrays me sort, toString, equals, copyOf aur binarySearch ready hain — haath se likhne se safer.
analogy: Array ek train ke reserved seats jaisa hai: seats ki ginti fix hai, har seat ka number zero se shuru hota hai, aur aap seedha seat number se pahunchte ho. 2D array ek sleeper coach hai — har bay (row) me alag number of berths ho sakte hain.
why: Arrays are the base of collections, strings, images, matrices and every interview data-structure question. Understanding length, indexing and copies prevents the most common runtime crash in beginner Java code.

syntax.code:
int[] marks = new int[4];        // 0, 0, 0, 0
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7};      // literal
String[] names = new String[2];    // null, null
System.out.println(marks.length); // 4
System.out.println(names[0] == null); // true
syntax.note: length is a field on arrays, not a method. Object arrays default to null; numeric arrays default to 0.
Each row has its own length, so the inner condition uses grid[r].length, not grid[0].length.

topics.title: Declaration and initialisation
topics.body: Type[] name = new Type[size] or a literal {…}. Arrays are objects on the heap; the variable holds a reference. Uninitialised numeric elements are 0, booleans false, references null.

topics.title: Traversal and the length field
topics.body: Indexes run 0..length-1. A for-each loop is cleaner for reading values; a classic for gives you the index. Use array.length (field) for arrays and text.length() (method) for Strings.

topics.title: Searching
topics.body: Linear search checks each element: O(n) and works on unsorted data. Binary search is O(log n) but needs a sorted array; Arrays.binarySearch returns the index or a negative insertion point.

topics.title: Sorting
topics.body: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n²) teaching algorithms. Arrays.sort uses a tuned dual-pivot quicksort for primitives and a stable merge sort for objects, and is what production code should call.

topics.title: 2D and jagged arrays
topics.body: int[][] is an array of int[]. new int[3][4] allocates every row; new int[3][] leaves rows null until you allocate them. Iterate rows, then columns of that row.

topics.title: Copying and Arrays utilities
topics.body: Arrays.copyOf copies with a new length, System.arraycopy copies ranges, and clone makes a shallow copy. Arrays.toString/equals/deepToString/fill/sort/binarySearch/stream cover most day-to-day needs.

topics.title: Debugging array code
topics.body: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException means an index was outside 0..length-1. Print length and the index just before the access. NullPointerException on a 2D row usually means the row was never allocated.

examples.title: Sum, average and maximum
lines: marks is a literal array of five ints; its length is fixed at 5.
max starts at marks[0] so it is valid even for all-negative arrays.
The for-each loop reads each value once, accumulating the sum and tracking the maximum.
Average casts sum to double before dividing, otherwise 396 / 5 would be 79.

examples.title: Jagged rows and row sums
examples.output:
row 0: [1, 2] sum=3
row 1: [3, 4, 5] sum=12
row 2: [6] sum=6
3 rows, last row length 1
lines: The outer loop walks three rows; each row is its own int array.
The inner for-each adds that row's values, whatever the row length is.
Arrays.toString prints the row contents in brackets without a loop of our own.
The last line reads the row count and the final row's length, which is 1 — proof the rows differ.

mistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i <= nums.length; i++) sum += nums[i];
mistakes.right: for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) sum += nums[i];
mistakes.why: <= reads one past the last valid index, which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Assignment copies the reference, so both variables point at the same array. Use copyOf or clone for a new array.

debug.brief: This sum loop crashes on the last element. Fix the boundary.
hints: The loop condition must be strictly less than length.

best: Prefer for-each for reading, indexed for when the position matters.
Use Arrays.sort instead of writing a sort in production code.
Copy arrays with Arrays.copyOf/clone; assignment only copies the reference.
tip: Interviewers ask linear versus binary search and expect the sorted precondition for binary search. Mention Arrays.binarySearch returns a negative value encoding the insertion point when the key is missing.
revision: Arrays are fixed-size, zero-indexed and use the length field.
Indexes 0..length-1; <= length is the classic crash.
2D arrays are arrays of arrays, so rows can be jagged.
Arrays.sort sorts in place; Arrays.toString prints contents.

practice.title: Reverse an array
practice.prompt: Reverse an int array in place with two pointers and print it.
practice.hint: Swap i and j, moving toward the middle.

practice.title: Second largest
practice.prompt: Find the second largest distinct value in an array in one pass.
practice.hint: Track largest and secondLargest; skip duplicates of largest.

practice.title: Matrix transpose
practice.prompt: Print the transpose of a 3×3 matrix.
practice.hint: Output row r, column c as input[c][r].

mcqs.q: What is the last valid index of int[] a = new int[5]?
mcqs.explain: Indexes run 0..length-1, so the last is 4.

mcqs.q: Which prints an array's contents readably?
mcqs.explain: Arrays.toString formats elements; printing the array directly prints a type@hash code.
Binary search halves the range using ordering, so the input must be sorted.

interview.a: Arrays are fixed-size and can hold primitives; ArrayList is resizable, holds objects only (with autoboxing for primitives) and offers add/remove. Arrays are faster and lighter when the size is known.
interview.followUp: Which is better for frequent insertions in the middle? (Neither is great — a linked list is O(1) at a known node, though arrays still win for most real access patterns.)

interview.q: How do you find the second largest element in one pass?
interview.a: Keep largest and secondLargest. For each value: if it is greater than largest, move largest into secondLargest and set largest; else if it is greater than secondLargest and not equal to largest, update secondLargest. O(n) time, O(1) space.
interview.followUp: What if all elements are equal? (No second largest exists; return a sentinel or throw, and say why.)

lab.title: Array sum and maximum
lab.brief: Read n, then n integers. Print the sum and the maximum on two lines.
hints: Start max at nums[0], not 0 — otherwise all-negative arrays fail.
Use a long sum if n can be large.
